analysis.one_liner: Repeals federal sugar price supports, quotas, and import tariffs that keep US sugar prices high.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Sen. Richard Lugar with 6 Republican cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee in March 2011 and died there without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would shut down the federal sugar program, which props up US sugar prices through government-backed loans, limits on how much sugar growers can sell, and steep import taxes and quotas. The result would be cheaper sugar for American households and food makers, and the end of a guaranteed revenue stream for sugar beet and cane growers. It was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee and never received any action.
analysis.who_benefits: American consumers, who pay more for sugar and sugary foods than consumers in most other countries because the federal program restricts supply and blocks cheaper imports. Food and beverage makers that buy sugar in bulk, including candy and baked-goods companies, would also gain from lower input costs.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the sugar loan program, ending federal price-support loans for the 2012 and later crops of sugarcane and sugar beets [S2][S3].
Terminates the marketing quotas and allotments that cap how much sugar domestic growers can sell, a supply restriction that keeps prices elevated [S3].
Eliminates the tariffs and over-quota tariff-rate quotas on imported cane and beet sugar, setting most sugar import rates to free and striking the quota-allocation note from the tariff schedule [S3].
Ends related supports including Section 32 sugar purchases, storage payments, storage facility loans, and the feedstock flexibility program for bioenergy producers [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Sugar beet and cane growers and processors, who would lose guaranteed minimum prices, protected market share, and insulation from foreign competition, and the rural sugar-producing regions that depend on that income.

drawbacks.text: Growers would face immediate exposure to world market prices with no phase-out: the bill applies to the 2012 crop, which could cut grower incomes abruptly and hurt sugar-producing rural communities [S3].

Supporters of the sugar program argue that world sugar prices are themselves distorted by foreign subsidies, so unilateral free trade could let subsidized foreign sugar undercut US growers rather than deliver lasting savings to consumers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers a clear, broad benefit — lower sugar prices for every household and food buyer — at the cost of narrowing it to one crop sector that has been federally protected since the 1930s. The abruptness is a legitimate objection: ending loans, quotas, and tariffs all at once with no transition aid is a shock to growers. But the program it ends functions as a persistent tax on the food budget of ordinary Americans in favor of a small, concentrated group of producers, and the bill's flaw is design speed, not direction.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never acted on it, so the bill expired when the 112th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Richard Lugar introduced the Free Sugar Act of 2011 on March 30, 2011, joined by Sen. Ron Paul, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry [S1][S3][S5].
Six Republican senators cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did [S4].
The Agriculture Committee took no further action — no markup, no hearing, no vote — and the bill died at the end of the 112th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: US sugar beet and cane growers and processors, who kept their price supports, sales quotas, and tariff protection for another farm bill cycle, while consumers continued paying above-world prices for sugar.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Sugar growers, who kept their federal program

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 6 cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and a Democratic-led Agriculture Committee never acted on the bill.

industries.industry: US sugar beet and cane growers and processors
industries.note: The sugar program guarantees them supported prices, limits competing supply through marketing allotments, and shields them from imports with steep tariffs — the mechanism that keeps US sugar prices above world levels. The bill would end all three, so the industry's interest runs directly against consumers' interest in cheaper sugar.

industries.industry: Food and beverage manufacturers (candy, baked goods, cereals)
industries.note: These companies buy sugar in bulk and pay more for it under the current program; the bill would cut a major input cost, savings that would partly flow to shoppers.

industries.industry: Sugar importers and foreign sugar producers
industries.note: Eliminating the tariffs and over-quota rates would let them sell into the US market on equal terms, increasing supply and lowering prices.
